prompt:
In the grid below, draw horizontal and vertical segments of unit length joining pairs of adjacent dots (some have been given to you) so that

1. every dot is connected by line segments to exactly $1$ or $3$ adjacent dots,
2. any dot can be reached from any other dot by following a path of segments, and
3. no area is completely enclosed by segments.

Note: "Unit length" is the length between two adjacent dots when there is no missing dot between them. For example, we cannot draw a vertical line segment down from the dot in the top right corner because the length of this segment would be $2$ units.

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above. (Note: In any other USAMTS problem, you need to provide a full proof. Only in this problem is an answer without justification acceptable.)

solutions.title: A tree with all degrees odd
solutions.body:
Conditions 2 and 3 say the drawing is a **tree** on the $44$ dots: it is connected and has no cycles. So it has exactly $43$ segments. If $n_1$ dots have degree $1$ and $n_3$ have degree $3$, then $n_1 + n_3 = 44$ and $n_1 + 3n_3 = 2\cdot 43 = 86$, so $n_3 = 21$ and $n_1 = 23$.

Useful local facts:
- A dot with at most two possible neighbours must have degree exactly $1$.
- A dot that already has two segments must get exactly one more.
- A segment must never close a loop.
- A group of dots must never be cut off from the rest.

For example, the top-right dot has only one neighbour, so the segment to its left is forced. The bottom-left corner of the given "U" on the left already has two segments and its only other neighbour is the dot below it, so that segment is forced too. Continuing with such deductions leads to
$$\begin{array}{ccccccccccccc}\bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet \\  &  & \vert &  & \vert &  &  &  &  &  & \vert &  &  \\  &  & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  &  \\  &  &  &  & \vert &  &  &  &  &  & \vert &  &  \\ \bullet &  & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet \\ \vert &  & \vert &  & \vert &  &  &  & \vert &  & \vert &  &  \\ \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  &  \\ \vert &  &  &  &  &  & \vert &  &  &  & \vert &  &  \\ \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet \\ \vert &  &  &  &  &  & \vert &  & \vert &  & \vert &  &  \\ \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \bullet &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet \\ \vert &  & \vert &  &  &  &  &  & \vert &  &  &  &  \\ \bullet &  & \bullet &  &  &  & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet & \text{---} & \bullet &  & \end{array}$$
**Check.** There are $43$ segments, every dot has $1$ or $3$ segments ($23$ dots of degree $1$, $21$ of degree $3$), all $13$ given segments are used, and the drawing is connected. A connected graph with $44$ vertices and $43$ edges is a tree, so no area is enclosed. An exhaustive computer search confirms that this is the only solution.

**Answer:** the drawing above.

prompt:
Sydney the squirrel is at $(0, 0)$ and is trying to get to $(2021, 2022)$. She can move only by reflecting her position over any line that can be formed by connecting two lattice points, provided that the reflection puts her on another lattice point. Is it possible for Sydney to reach $(2021, 2022)$?

Lattice points are points in the Cartesian plane where both coordinates are integers.
answer: **No.** A reflection between lattice points of different parity of $x + y$ would need a mirror line with no lattice points, so the parity of $x + y$ never changes; $0 + 0$ is even, $2021 + 2022$ is odd.

solutions.title: Parity of $x + y$ is invariant
solutions.body:
Call a lattice point **even** or **odd** according to the parity of the sum of its coordinates.

Suppose one move takes Sydney from a lattice point $P = (p, q)$ to a lattice point $P' = (p + u, q + v)$, where $(u, v) \ne (0, 0)$. Then the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$, i.e. the set of points $(x, y)$ with
$$u\left(x - p - \tfrac u2\right) + v\left(y - q - \tfrac v2\right) = 0 \iff 2\big(u(x - p) + v(y - q)\big) = u^2 + v^2.$$
Now suppose $P$ and $P'$ have different parity, i.e. $u + v$ is odd. Then exactly one of $u, v$ is odd, so $u^2 + v^2$ is odd. For a lattice point $(x, y)$ the left-hand side is even, so **no** lattice point lies on this line. But Sydney may only reflect over lines through (two) lattice points. So every move keeps her on points of the same parity.

She starts at $(0, 0)$, which is even, while $2021 + 2022 = 4043$ is odd. So she can never reach $(2021, 2022)$.

**Answer: No.** ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $S$ be the set of $n^2$ cells in an $n \times n$ grid. Call a subset $T$ of $S$ a **double staircase** if

1. $T$ can be partitioned into $n$ horizontal nonoverlapping rectangles of dimensions $1 \times 1, 1 \times 2, \dots, 1 \times n$, and
2. $T$ can also be partitioned into $n$ vertical nonoverlapping rectangles of dimensions $1 \times 1, 2 \times 1, \dots, n \times 1$.

In terms of $n$, how many double staircases are there? (Rotations and reflections are considered distinct.)

An example of a double staircase when $n = 3$ is shown below.

solutions.title: Row and column lengths form "mountain" permutations
solutions.body:
**One tile per row and per column.** The $1 \times n$ tile fills a whole row, so every column meets $T$. There are $n$ vertical tiles and $n$ columns, and each vertical tile lies in a single column, so each column contains **exactly one** vertical tile. Hence each column of $T$ is one contiguous block. Likewise the $n \times 1$ tile shows that each row contains exactly one horizontal tile, so each row of $T$ is one contiguous block.

Let $h_1, \dots, h_n$ be the lengths of the row blocks (top to bottom) and $v_1, \dots, v_n$ those of the column blocks (left to right). Both are permutations of $1, \dots, n$.

**Call a permutation a *mountain* if no entry is smaller than both of its neighbours.** Equivalently, it increases up to $n$ and then decreases. The sequence $(h_i)$ must be a mountain. Indeed, suppose $h_j < h_i$ and $h_j < h_k$ with $i < j < k$, and say the $n$ lies at or before position $j$ (the other case is symmetric). Then the block in row $k$ is longer than the block in row $j$. So some column contains a cell of row $k$ but not of row $j$, and every column contains a cell of the full row (the row of $n$). Since that full row is above row $j$ and row $k$ is below it, this column has a cell, then a gap at row $j$, then a cell, contradicting that each column is one block. Similarly $(v_i)$ is a mountain.

**Counting mountains.** In a mountain of $1, \dots, k$ the entry $1$ must be at an end (otherwise it is smaller than both neighbours). Removing it and decreasing the other entries by $1$ gives a mountain of $1, \dots, k - 1$, and this is reversible. So there are $2^{k-1}$ mountains of length $k$.

**$T$ is determined by $(h, v)$.** We prove a stronger statement: any set of cells in an $n \times n$ grid whose row counts are a permutation $h$ of $1, \dots, n$ and whose column counts are a permutation $v$ of $1, \dots, n$ consists exactly of the cells $(i, j)$ with $h_i + v_j \ge n + 1$. Use induction on $n$; the cases $n = 0, 1$ are clear.
- The row with count $n$ and the column with count $n$ are full.
- Delete them. Every other row and column loses exactly one cell, so the counts become permutations of $0, \dots, n - 2$.
- The row and column with count $0$ are now empty. Before the deletion they had count $1$, and their only cell was in the full column (respectively, full row).
- Delete them as well. This leaves an $(n - 2) \times (n - 2)$ grid whose row and column counts are permutations of $1, \dots, n - 2$, namely $h_i - 1$ and $v_j - 1$.

By induction the remaining cells are those with $(h_i - 1) + (v_j - 1) \ge (n - 2) + 1$, i.e. $h_i + v_j \ge n + 1$. The deleted rows and columns also satisfy this rule: a full row has $h_i = n$, and a count-$1$ row meets only the column with $v_j = n$.

**Every pair of mountains occurs.** Given mountains $h$ and $v$, let $T$ be the set of cells with $h_i + v_j \ge n + 1$. Row $i$ consists of the $h_i$ columns with the largest values $v_j \ge n + 1 - h_i$. In a mountain the $k$ largest entries always occupy consecutive positions, so this row is a single block of length $h_i$. Likewise each column $j$ is a single block of length $v_j$. So the rows give a partition into tiles $1 \times 1, \dots, 1 \times n$ and the columns give one into $1 \times 1, \dots, n \times 1$, and $T$ is a double staircase.

Hence the number of double staircases is $\left(2^{n-1}\right)^2 = 4^{n-1}$. A brute-force count gives $1, 4, 16, 64$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$.

**Answer:** $4^{n-1}$.

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle whose vertices are inside a circle $\Omega$. Prove that we can choose two of the vertices of $ABC$ such that there are infinitely many circles $\omega$ that satisfy the following properties:

1. $\omega$ is inside of $\Omega$,
2. $\omega$ passes through the two chosen vertices, and
3. the third vertex is in the interior of $\omega$.
answer: Let $C$ be the vertex farthest from the centre $O$ and shrink the circle centred at $O$ through $C$ by homotheties at $C$ until it first meets $A$ or $B$ (say $B$). That circle lies inside $\Omega$, passes through $B$ and $C$, and contains $A$ in its interior, so small perturbations among circles through $B$ and $C$ give infinitely many. If $A$ and $B$ are met at the same time, the circumcircle lies inside $\Omega$ and we perturb it among circles through $A$ and $B$.

solutions.title: Shrink a circle about the farthest vertex
solutions.body:
Let $O$ and $R$ be the centre and radius of $\Omega$. Label the vertices so that $OA, OB \le OC$. Then $OC < R$.

**A perturbation fact.** Suppose a circle $\omega_0$ passes through two vertices, has the third vertex strictly inside, and lies in the open disk of $\Omega$. Then infinitely many circles have the same three properties. Indeed, move the centre of $\omega_0$ slightly along the perpendicular bisector of the two chosen vertices, keeping the circle through them. The radius changes continuously. Since $\omega_0$ has positive distance both from $\Omega$ and from the third vertex, all sufficiently small moves still give circles inside $\Omega$ containing the third vertex in their interior.

**Shrinking.** Let $\gamma$ be the circle with centre $O$ through $C$. Its disk lies inside the open disk of $\Omega$, because its radius is $OC < R$, and $A$, $B$ lie in its closed disk. For $0 < r \le 1$ let $D_r$ be the image of this closed disk under the homothety with centre $C$ and ratio $r$. The $D_r$ are nested: $D_r \subset D_{r'}$ for $r < r'$, and their boundary circles meet only at $C$. They all lie inside $\gamma$'s disk, and they shrink to the point $C$ as $r \to 0$. Let $r_A$ be the smallest $r$ with $A \in D_r$ (so $A$ lies on the boundary circle of $D_{r_A}$), and define $r_B$ similarly. Both are positive since $A, B \ne C$.

**Case $r_A \ne r_B$**, say $r_A < r_B$. The boundary circle $\gamma'$ of $D_{r_B}$ passes through $B$ and $C$. It also contains $A$ in its interior: $A \in D_{r_A}$, and $D_{r_A}$ touches the boundary of $D_{r_B}$ only at $C \ne A$. And $\gamma'$ lies inside $\Omega$. By the perturbation fact we get infinitely many circles through $B$ and $C$ with $A$ inside.

**Case $r_A = r_B$.** Then $A$, $B$, $C$ all lie on the boundary circle of $D_{r_A}$, which is therefore the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of $ABC$, and $\Gamma$ lies strictly inside $\Omega$. Now use circles through $A$ and $B$. Choose coordinates with $A = (-1, 0)$ and $B = (1, 0)$, with $C$ above the $x$-axis ($y_C > 0$). The circle through $A$, $B$ with centre $(0, t)$ contains a point $(x, y)$ in its interior iff
$$x^2 + (y - t)^2 < 1 + t^2 \iff x^2 + y^2 - 1 - 2ty < 0.$$
For $C$ the left side is $0$ at $t = t_0$ (the circumcircle) and strictly decreasing in $t$, because $y_C > 0$. So for every $t > t_0$, $C$ is strictly inside. Since $\Gamma$ lies strictly inside $\Omega$, all $t$ slightly larger than $t_0$ give circles inside $\Omega$. That is infinitely many circles through $A$ and $B$ containing $C$.

In every case a suitable pair of vertices exists. ∎

answer: If $d$ is an integer, $e = a + b\lfloor c\rfloor$ and $f = bd$ work, by $\lfloor \lfloor y\rfloor / d\rfloor = \lfloor y/d\rfloor$. Conversely, comparing growth rates forces $f = bd$, and the set where both sides equal $k$ has length $f = bd$ on the right and $b$ times an integer on the left, so $d$ is an integer.

solutions.title: Compare slopes, then lengths of level sets
solutions.body:
Let $L(x)$ and $R(x)$ denote the left and right sides.

**If $d$ is a positive integer.** We use the standard fact that $\left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor y\rfloor}{q} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{y}{q} \right\rfloor$ for every real $y$ and positive integer $q$. To see it, write $\lfloor y\rfloor = kq + s$ with $0 \le s \le q - 1$; then $kq \le y < kq + s + 1 \le (k + 1)q$.

Let $N = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a}{b} \right\rfloor$, an integer. Then:
- $\left\lfloor \frac{N + c}{d} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor N + c\rfloor}{d} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{N + \lfloor c\rfloor}{d} \right\rfloor$.
- Since $\lfloor c\rfloor$ is an integer, $N + \lfloor c\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a + b\lfloor c\rfloor}{b} \right\rfloor$.
- Applying the fact again with $q = d$,
$$L(x) = \left\lfloor \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{x + a + b\lfloor c\rfloor}{b} \right\rfloor}{d} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a + b\lfloor c\rfloor}{bd} \right\rfloor.$$

So $e = a + b\lfloor c\rfloor > 0$ and $f = bd > 0$ work.

**If $e, f$ exist.** First, $f = bd$. Take $x = Nb - a$ with $N$ an integer. Then $L = \left\lfloor \frac{N + c}{d} \right\rfloor$ and $R = \left\lfloor \frac{Nb - a + e}{f} \right\rfloor$. Equal floors have arguments differing by less than $1$, so
$$\left| N\left(\frac1d - \frac bf\right) + \frac cd - \frac{e - a}{f} \right| < 1 \quad\text{for all integers } N.$$
This forces $\frac1d = \frac bf$, i.e. $f = bd$.

Now fix an integer $k$ and compare the sets where each side equals $k$. The set $\{x : R(x) = k\}$ is the interval $[kf - e, (k + 1)f - e)$, of length $f = bd$. On the other hand, $L(x) = k$ iff the integer $N = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a}{b} \right\rfloor$ satisfies $kd - c \le N < kd - c + d$. Each value of $N$ corresponds to an interval of $x$ of length $b$, and consecutive values give adjacent intervals. So $\{x : L(x) = k\}$ is an interval of length $b \cdot j_k$, where $j_k$ is the number of integers in $[kd - c, kd - c + d)$.

The two sets are equal, so $b\, j_k = bd$, i.e. $d = j_k$ is an integer. ∎
